references.text: Earlier in the same sending speech, Jesus says that the disciples should not greet anyone along the way, which underscores the same urgency and focus in the mission that underlies the instruction to eat what is set before them.

Jesus instructs the disciples to stay in the house that receives them and to eat and drink what they are given, because the worker is worthy of his wages. Verse 8 extends this from a house to a city – the principle of accepting what is offered also applies when an entire city receives them.

Contrast verses describing what the disciples should do when a city does not receive them – they are to go out and shake the dust off their feet. This is the opposite of verse 8, where the city receives them.
In the sending of the twelve, Jesus gives a similar instruction to stay in the house they come to, which reflects the same practice of hospitality as in Luke 10:8.

Paul advises eating what is set before one without raising questions for conscience's sake. The principle of eating what is offered without being picky has a parallel to Jesus' instruction in Luke 10:8.
In Matthew's version of the sending speech, Jesus gives similar instructions to find a worthy person in the city and stay there. The context of being received in a city is the same.
Abraham offers hospitality to the three guests and says they may refresh themselves with food. Accepting what is set before one by a hospitable host is an Old Testament principle of hospitality.
Jesus sends out the twelve and says that they have received for free and should give for free – the principle of reciprocity in service and receiving underlies the instruction to accept hospitality.
The widow of Zarephath sets before Elijah what little she has, and he eats what is offered. The prophet's acceptance of hospitality is an Old Testament parallel to Jesus' instruction.
